overview:
Türkiye, also written Turkey in English, straddles two continents: a small European corner called Thrace and the much larger Asian peninsula of Anatolia, divided by narrow straits and the Sea of Marmara. It borders eight countries, from Greece and Bulgaria in the west to Georgia, Armenia, Iran, Iraq and Syria in the east, and has coasts on the Black, Aegean and Mediterranean seas. At about 784,000 km² it is roughly twice the size of Germany.

About 85 million people live here, speaking Turkish, with Kurdish spoken by a large minority in the southeast. Ankara, in the center of Anatolia, is the capital, while Istanbul, on the Bosphorus strait, is the largest city and the only major city in the world standing on two continents.

Türkiye is a presidential republic. It is known for its food, its carpets, its ancient ruins and its landscapes of cotton-white terraces and fairy-chimney rocks.
landAndNature: Most of Türkiye is a high plateau ringed by mountains, rising in the east to Mount Ararat, a snow-capped volcanic cone of 5,137 meters. The Tigris and Euphrates rivers both begin here. In Cappadocia, soft volcanic rock has eroded into tall cones and pillars that people hollowed into houses, churches and whole underground cities; hot-air balloons drift over them at dawn. At Pamukkale, mineral-rich hot springs have built a hillside of dazzling white limestone terraces filled with warm water. Coastlines range from pine-backed Mediterranean coves to the humid, tea-growing Black Sea hills. The country sits on major fault lines and suffers severe earthquakes, including a devastating one in 2023. Brown bears, wolves, wild goats and loggerhead turtles all live here.
peopleAndCulture: Turkish food is one of the world's great cuisines: kebabs and meze, stuffed vine leaves, pide flatbreads, baklava layered with pistachios, and thick coffee whose grounds are sometimes read for fortunes. Tea, served in tulip-shaped glasses, is drunk all day. Hospitality is a point of honor; a guest is offered food before anything else. Most Turks are Muslim, and the country's government is officially secular. Oil wrestling, in which competitors coated in olive oil grapple at Kırkpınar, has been held for over 650 years, and soccer draws enormous crowds. Turkish carpets, ceramics from İznik, and shadow puppet plays are old arts, and the whirling dervishes of Konya spin in a meditative ceremony descended from the poet Rumi.
history: Anatolia holds some of humanity's oldest settlements: Göbekli Tepe's carved stone circles are about 11,500 years old, older than farming. Hittites, Greeks, Persians and Romans ruled in turn, and Constantinople, founded in 330, became the capital of the Byzantine empire for over a thousand years. Turkic peoples moved in from Central Asia, and in 1453 the Ottomans took Constantinople, building an empire that stretched across the Middle East, North Africa and southeastern Europe. During World War I the Ottoman government carried out mass killings and deportations of its Armenian population beginning in 1915, in which around a million or more people died; most historians and many countries recognize this as genocide, while Türkiye's government disputes that term. The empire collapsed after the war, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk founded a republic in 1923, changing the alphabet, calendar and laws.
funFacts: Istanbul is the only major city in the world built on two continents, linked by bridges across the Bosphorus.
Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Türkiye has carved stone pillars about 11,500 years old, built before pottery or farming.
Beneath Cappadocia lie underground cities, one with at least eight levels that sheltered thousands of people.
Türkiye grows about 70 percent of the world's hazelnuts, mostly on the steep Black Sea coast.
Oil wrestling at Kırkpınar has been contested every year since 1346, making it one of the oldest sporting events anywhere.
